phrases.translation: Blessed is the One Who
phrases.explanation: The surah opens with a declaration of blessing, and the commentary explains the word as a form derived from blessing, used of Allah in the sense that He is sanctified and exalted. The blessing is attached to an act rather than to an object, which makes it a statement about what Allah has done. What follows in the chapter is then presented as the fruit of that act rather than as a new subject.

phrases.translation: sent down the Standard
phrases.explanation: The act itself is the sending down of the Criterion, the name given to the revelation because it separates truth from falsehood, one surah after another. The commentary explains the sending as a distinction drawn for people who would otherwise be unable to tell the two apart. The name suits the chapter, which spends much of its length answering objections and separating true claims from false ones.

phrases.translation: to His servant,
phrases.explanation: The revelation comes down upon a servant, and the commentary keeps the title as it stands rather than softening it. Being sent to a servant says something about both ends of the transaction, since the One who sends is the Lord and the one who receives is owned. The word also prepares for the objection that follows, where the messenger's ordinary human life is treated as a reason to doubt him.

phrases.translation: so that he may be a warner to the whole world
phrases.explanation: The purpose is stated as warning. The messenger is to be a warner to the whole world, and the commentary explains this as calling all jinn and men to Allah and warning them of His punishment if they do not affirm His oneness and purify their worship. The scope is universal, so no community can treat the message as someone else's business. Warning is the first note of the surah, and mercy is named later.

phrases.translation: ˹Allah is˺ the One to Whom belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes the One who sent the Criterion. The kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, and the commentary explains this as His sovereignty, with His command and decree carried out by the whole of creation. The practical conclusion is stated directly, that the inhabitants of the kingdom should obey Him and not rebel. The argument of the surah rests on this ownership, since a servant's duty follows from belonging to a master.

phrases.translation: Who has never had ˹any˺ offspring,
phrases.explanation: The first denial concerns offspring. He has never had a child, and the commentary explains this as a refutation of those who ascribed a child to Allah and said that the angels were His daughters. The verse does not argue the point here but states it as a fact that exposes the claim. The surah returns to the same accusation later, when the idolaters are asked about those they worshipped.

phrases.translation: nor does He have a partner in ˹governing˺ the kingdom.
phrases.explanation: The second denial is that He has no partner in the kingdom. The commentary reports the polytheists' own formula, in which they admitted a partner belonging to Allah while claiming to possess him and what he possessed. The verse answers that formula by denying that any such partner exists. What they had attached to their pilgrimage cry is thus stripped away, and the worship built on it loses its foundation.

phrases.translation: He has created everything,
phrases.explanation: The verse then states what the Owner has done. He created everything, and the commentary explains this as the reason worship belongs to Him alone, since all things are His creation and His property. Idols, angels, jinn, and men are all included in that creation. The surah's argument rests here, because what is created cannot be the equal of the One who made it.

phrases.translation: ordaining it precisely
phrases.explanation: The final phrase adds measure to creation. Everything has been ordained precisely, and the commentary explains this as each thing being set to suit that for which it is fit, with neither deficiency nor disparity. The pair, created and measured, also answers the charge that the revelation was improvised. A Maker who orders what He makes is consistent in what He sends down.

phrases.translation: Yet they have taken besides Him gods
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to what the polytheists set beside Him. They have taken gods besides Him, and the commentary identifies these as idols they fashioned with their own hands and then worshipped. The reproach is addressed to people of sound reason who nevertheless followed a way that none but the confused would tread. The surah is not merely disagreeing with them but expressing astonishment at them.

phrases.translation: who cannot create anything but are themselves created.
phrases.explanation: The first charge against these gods is that they create nothing while being created themselves. The order of the sentence matters, since the very thing they were relied on for is the one thing they cannot do. Nothing about them is original, since they were made before they were worshipped. What is depended on is therefore less capable than the people depending on it.

phrases.translation: Nor can they protect or benefit themselves.
phrases.explanation: The next charge removes even the appearance of self-interest. They cannot protect or benefit themselves, and the commentary explains this as their inability to draw any good toward themselves or to ward off harm from one who intends it. A deity that cannot look after itself cannot look after anyone else. The verse keeps the argument at the level of the obvious, where the idol's helplessness is plain to anyone who thinks.

phrases.translation: Nor can they control life, death, or resurrection
phrases.explanation: The last charge narrows the comparison to the matters that count. These gods cannot control life, death, or resurrection, and the commentary explains the resurrection as the raising of the dead to life after death. These are precisely the affairs at stake in the surah, which is largely about the Hour and the return to Allah. The idols are absent from every stage of the journey they were supposed to assist.

phrases.translation: The disbelievers say, “This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but a fabrication
phrases.explanation: The verse reports the first of a series of accusations against the revelation. The disbelievers say that the Qur'an is nothing but a fabrication, and the commentary explains the word as a lie which Muhammad had invented. The charge is that the message is human in origin. The surah has just described the One who sent it down, so the objection is set against that description rather than answered in the abstract.

phrases.translation: which he made up with the help of others.”
phrases.explanation: The accusation also names accomplices. They claim that others helped him, and the commentary reports that they meant the Jews, who were said to teach him what he brought. The claim is that the revelation is borrowed rather than received. This allows the objectors to explain away both its content and its coherence, since a text assembled from elsewhere would be neither fresh nor consistent.

phrases.translation: Their claim is totally unjustified and untrue
phrases.explanation: The verse then answers the charge. Their claim is unjustified and untrue, and the commentary explains the wrongdoing as putting a thing in the wrong place, since they described the word of Allah with an attribute that did not belong to it. The falsehood is named as a making fair-seeming of what is not true. The judgement is brief because the surah goes on to expose the accusation in detail.

phrases.translation: And they say, “˹These revelations are only˺ ancient fables
phrases.explanation: A second charge follows the first. They say the revelation consists of ancient fables, and the commentary identifies the speaker as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who had travelled to al-Hira, learned the tales of the Persian kings, and repeated them to the Quraysh while claiming to tell better stories than Muhammad. The accusation is therefore not disinterested, since it came from a man offering a rival entertainment.

phrases.translation: which he has had written down,
phrases.explanation: The fables are said to have been written down for him, and the commentary explains the phrase as their claim that these tales were copied from the books of the Jews and dictated to him. Writing is named to make the borrowing sound deliberate. The charge turns a text recited from memory into a document passed from hand to hand, which is what the objectors needed it to be.

phrases.translation: and they are rehearsed to him morning and evening.”
phrases.explanation: The times named are morning and evening, and the commentary explains the phrase as dictation repeated at those hours. The detail is meant to suggest a routine of instruction rather than an act of revelation. Recitation at fixed times looks ordinary to anyone watching, and the objectors use that ordinariness against him. The verse preserves the accusation in their own words.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “This ˹Quran˺ has been revealed
phrases.explanation: The answer begins with a command to speak. Say that this Qur'an has been revealed, and the commentary explains this as a direct denial of the claim that it is fables or something he invented with help. The reply does not defend the messenger's circumstances but names the source of the book. Everything that follows in the verse explains what kind of source that is.

phrases.translation: by the One Who knows the secrets of the heavens and the earth.
phrases.explanation: The source is the One who knows the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and the commentary explains this as the One from whom nothing is hidden, who tallies what people conceal and requites them for it. The argument rests on knowledge, since a book that speaks to what is hidden could only come from the One who knows it. The claim of borrowing is answered at its root rather than piece by piece.

phrases.translation: Surely He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with forgiveness and mercy. The commentary explains that Allah does not cease to forgive His creation and show them mercy, and that this is why He grants them time despite their falsehood and unbelief. The rebuke is therefore not followed by a threat, and the delay in punishment is offered as evidence of patience. The names chosen here answer the accusation of invention with generosity rather than severity.

phrases.translation: And they say ˹mockingly˺, “What kind of messenger is this who eats food
phrases.explanation: Another objection is reported, and it concerns the messenger's body. What kind of messenger is this who eats food? The commentary explains that the questioners expected a messenger to be above ordinary needs, and reports their demand for an angel who would confirm him and answer on his behalf. Their assumption is that a man who is hungry cannot be sent by God, which the surah has already contradicted by calling him a servant.

phrases.translation: and goes about in market-places ˹for a living˺?
phrases.explanation: The second half of the complaint concerns work. He goes about in the market-places for a living, and the commentary reports the leaders of Quraysh pointing out that he walked in the markets and sought his livelihood as they did. The verse names the place where a messenger's humanity is hardest to hide. Ordinary commerce becomes, in their eyes, evidence against a claim to revelation.

phrases.translation: If only an angel had been sent down with him to be his co-warner
phrases.explanation: They then propose a test. If only an angel had been sent down with him to be his co-warner, and the commentary explains the requested angel as one who would confirm him in what he said and answer on his behalf. An angel would settle the question of authority, since nobody would dare to argue with a heavenly witness. The request is for proof that needs no trust, which is exactly what they were being asked to give.

phrases.translation: or a treasure had been cast down to him,
phrases.explanation: The demands continue with treasure. Perhaps a treasure should be cast down to him, and the commentary explains the treasure as gold or silver that would free him from seeking a livelihood. The request treats provision as the sign of rank. Beneath the mockery is the assumption that divine favour must be visible in comfort, and that a messenger without means cannot be genuine.

phrases.translation: or he had had a garden from which he may eat!”
phrases.explanation: A garden is then requested, one from which he might eat. Reciters differed over whether the word is read in the singular or the plural, and the commentary prefers the reading in which he is the one who eats, since the demand was for his benefit rather than theirs. A garden producing food would make the messenger independent. The complaint is not that they were hungry but that he was not visibly distinguished from them.

phrases.translation: And the wrongdoers say ˹to the believers˺, “You are only following a bewitched man.”
phrases.explanation: The verse then reports what the wrongdoers said to those who believed. They told them that they were following only a bewitched man, and the commentary explains the accusation as their claim that no sensible person would follow someone whose mind was taken over. The charge shifts from the messenger's lifestyle to the sanity of his followers. Its purpose is to shame them out of their faith.

phrases.translation: See ˹O Prophet˺ how they call you names!
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to look at what they are doing. See how they call you names, the verse says, and the commentary explains this as the comparisons they coined for him when they called him a bewitched man. The command to see turns an insult into an object lesson. What is being observed is not the wound it causes but the intellectual position from which it comes.

phrases.translation: So they have gone so ˹far˺ astray that they cannot find the ˹Right˺ Way
phrases.explanation: The consequence is then stated. They have gone so far astray that they cannot find the right way, and the commentary explains that they have missed the path of guidance and cannot reach the truth except through what he brought and from the direction they abandoned. Their mockery is presented as evidence of their confusion, and the surah treats the inability to find the way as the real misfortune.

phrases.translation: Blessed is the One Who—if He wills—can give you far better than ˹all˺ that:
phrases.explanation: The answer to the demands begins with a declaration of blessing. Allah, if He wills, can give the Prophet far better than all that they asked for. The commentary notes disagreement over what the word refers to, whether the treasure, the markets, or the whole of their demands, and it prefers the view that Allah promised something better than what the polytheists held in high regard. Nothing is refused as impossible.

phrases.translation: gardens under which rivers flow,
phrases.explanation: The first element of the better gift is gardens under which rivers flow, and the commentary explains them as orchards with rivers running at the roots of the trees. The image answers the single garden they had demanded with many, and it answers the wish for a livelihood with a provision that needs no labour. What they treated as the proof of rank is offered instead as a gift from Allah.

phrases.translation: and palaces as well
phrases.explanation: The palaces complete the answer, and the commentary explains them as built dwellings rather than tents or temporary shelters. The word is chosen because it replies to the demand for treasure and a garden with something more permanent. The promise is left conditional on Allah's will, which keeps it from becoming a debt owed to the messenger and keeps him from being diminished by what was withheld in this life.

phrases.translation: In fact, they deny the Hour.
phrases.explanation: The verse names the real reason for the rejection. It is not that the messenger eats or trades, but that they deny the Hour, and the commentary explains this as their refusal to believe in resurrection and in the recompense and punishment that follow. The objection about markets was a pretext. What they were actually unwilling to accept was that they would be raised and judged.

phrases.translation: And for the deniers of the Hour, We have prepared a blazing Fire
phrases.explanation: The penalty is then named. For those who deny the Hour, a blazing fire has been prepared, and the commentary explains this as a fire that flares over those who reject the raising of the dead. The preparation is stated in the past tense, which makes it sound already done. The verse thus answers the earlier demand for a sign by pointing to one that nobody would want to see.

phrases.translation: Once it sees them from a distance,
phrases.explanation: The fire is described as if it were a creature with a temper. When it sees them from a distance, they hear it fuming, and the commentary explains the word as the fire kindling its rage against them, its boiling and seething. The image gives the fire a will of its own. Distance does not protect them, because it perceives them before they arrive.

phrases.translation: they will hear it fuming and growling
phrases.explanation: The second sound is a hoarse groaning, and the commentary explains it as the noise the fire makes as it blazes. It also answers the obvious objection about hearing something invisible, noting that they hear the sound of its raging through its burning. The description is sensory rather than legal, so the warning lands as an experience before it lands as a doctrine.

phrases.translation: And when they are tossed into a narrow place inside ˹Hell˺, chained together,
phrases.explanation: The scene moves inside the fire. Those who denied the Hour are thrown into a narrow place within it, chained together, and the commentary explains the chains as their hands bound to their necks. Two kinds of pressure are described at once, the cramped space and the binding. Being crowded together offers no comfort, since each is restrained and cannot turn to another for help.

phrases.translation: then and there they will cry out for ˹instant˺ destruction
phrases.explanation: In that condition they cry out, and what they call for is destruction rather than rescue. The commentary records two explanations of the word, one that it means woe or ruin and the other that it means perishing outright. Either way they are asking to be ended. The cry shows how completely their earlier confidence has collapsed, since the people who denied the raising of the dead now beg for their own extinction.

phrases.translation: ˹They will be told,˺ “Do not cry only once for destruction,
phrases.explanation: The answer refuses even that request in the form they made it. They are told not to cry for destruction once, and the commentary explains the phrasing as a refusal to let them settle for a single appeal. The word used for destruction is a verbal noun, which cannot be counted, so the point is not arithmetic but intensity. Their wish to be finished is turned into an endless repetition of the wish.

phrases.translation: but cry many times over!”
phrases.explanation: Instead, they are told to cry many times over. The commentary explains this as an invitation to call for ruin repeatedly, since the noun cannot be pluralised and its frequency must be conveyed another way. The sentence is bitter rather than generous. What they wanted as an escape becomes a permanent condition, and the verse ends on the sound of voices that will not be answered.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Is this better
phrases.explanation: A question is put to the deniers, and it asks them to compare. Is this better? The word points back to the fire just described, with its narrow place and its chains. The verse does not answer for them but leaves the choice of comparison in their hands, since the alternative is about to be named. The question assumes that once both ends are set side by side the answer is obvious.

phrases.translation: or the Garden of Eternity which the righteous have been promised, as a reward and ˹an ultimate˺ destination
phrases.explanation: The alternative is the Garden of Eternity, promised to the righteous as a reward and a destination, and the commentary explains it as the garden whose delight endures and never perishes. It is promised to those who feared Allah in the world by obeying what He commanded and avoiding what He forbade. The wording reward and destination covers both what the garden is and what it does, since it repays a life and receives a person.

phrases.translation: There they will have whatever they wish for, forever.
phrases.explanation: The verse describes the life inside that garden. Whatever they wish for is theirs, and they remain there forever, and the commentary explains this as all that the soul desires and the eye delights in, with no departure and no loss of pleasure. The absence of limits is the point. What the people of the fire could not obtain for a moment is granted to these without end.

phrases.translation: That is a promise ˹to be sought after˺, binding on your Lord.”
phrases.explanation: The promise is then described in a striking phrase. It is a promise to be sought after, binding on your Lord, and the commentary explains this as a promise that is asked for and therefore owed, since the believers had asked their Lord for it. One early authority compared it to a debt that must be paid. The verse thus gives the believers assurance that their hope rests on something Allah has taken upon Himself.

phrases.translation: ˹Watch for˺ the Day He will gather them along with what they used to worship besides Allah,
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to a scene of accounting. On the Day Allah gathers the deniers together with what they used to worship besides Him, and the commentary explains the gathered objects as the angels, men, and jinn they had worshipped. It also notes a difference among reciters over whether the verse reads He gathers or We gather, and accepts both as sound. The point is that the worshipped will be present when the worshippers are questioned.

phrases.translation: and ask ˹the objects of worship˺, “Was it you who misled these servants of Mine,
phrases.explanation: The question is then put to those objects of worship rather than to the idolaters. Was it you who misled these servants of Mine? The commentary explains the question as asking whether they called those people away from guidance and into error until they perished. The framing matters, since it treats the worshippers as servants of Allah even while they were astray. It also gives the worshipped a chance to answer for themselves.

phrases.translation: or did they stray from the Way ˹on their own˺?”
phrases.explanation: The second half of the question offers them the alternative. Or did they stray from the way on their own? The commentary explains this as asking whether the servants themselves abandoned right guidance and turned toward ruin. The two possibilities cover the whole ground of responsibility, either the worshipped led them or they went by themselves. Nothing is left that would allow the blame to disappear between the two parties.

phrases.translation: They will say, “Glory be to You!
phrases.explanation: The answer begins with the declaration of Allah's glory, and the commentary identifies the speakers as the angels, together with Jesus and whoever else was worshipped among the believers. Beginning with glory rather than with denial puts the rejection of the false claim in the right order. They are not defending themselves so much as clearing the name of Allah from what was attributed to Him.

phrases.translation: It was not right for ˹others like˺ us to take any lords besides You,
phrases.explanation: They then deny that the worship was ever theirs to accept. It was not right for others like us to take any lords besides You, and the commentary explains this as their declaring themselves free of having any protector other than Allah. It notes a difference among reciters over the form of the verb, one reading making the worshipped deny taking protectors and the other making them deny any right to be worshipped. Both readings reject the same thing.

phrases.translation: but You allowed enjoyment for them and their forefathers ˹for so long˺
phrases.explanation: The next words explain how the error happened. You allowed enjoyment for them and their forefathers, and the commentary explains this as Allah providing them in this life with wealth and health. The verse names a cause rather than an excuse, since the enjoyment was given and not seized. Comfort that lasts is described here as the condition in which people lose their sense of need.

phrases.translation: that they forgot ˹Your˺ remembrance and became a doomed people.”
phrases.explanation: The result of that long enjoyment is then stated. They forgot Your remembrance and became a doomed people, and the commentary explains the last word as a people ruined and emptied, upon whom calamity and abandonment had settled. Forgetting is presented as the fruit of ease rather than of argument. The verse closes the exchange by naming what the worshippers became, not what their gods did to them.

phrases.translation: ˹The doomed will be told˺, “Your gods have clearly denied your claims.
phrases.explanation: The verse addresses the worshippers directly. Your gods have clearly denied your claims, and the commentary explains this as the objects of worship disowning the worship that had been offered to them. The word clearly makes the disowning public rather than private. What the idolaters had relied on as intercessors has now testified against them in front of everyone.

phrases.translation: So now you can neither ward off ˹the punishment˺ nor get any help.”
phrases.explanation: The consequence is then stated in two parts. They can neither ward off the punishment nor get any help, and the commentary keeps both refusals in view, since the gods cannot avert what is coming and cannot assist anyone against it. The verse removes the two things that worship of intermediaries was meant to secure. Their religion is shown to fail at exactly the point where it was supposed to work.

phrases.translation: And whoever of you does wrong, We will make them taste a horrible punishment
phrases.explanation: A warning is then added for the believers, and it is addressed to whoever among you does wrong. The commentary explains the wrong here as setting up a partner alongside Allah, which is to wrong oneself, and the punishment as the same great torment just described. The verse keeps the warning inside the community. Nobody is safe simply by belonging, since the standard applies to whoever commits the act.

phrases.translation: We never sent any messenger before you ˹O Prophet˺, who did not eat food and go about in market-places.
phrases.explanation: The verse answers the objection about the messenger's ordinary life. No messenger before him was sent who did not eat food and walk in the market-places, and the commentary presents this as a standing pattern rather than an exception. The objection assumed that a messenger should be exempt from human needs. The verse replies that every messenger shared them, so the objection would abolish the whole line of prophets.

phrases.translation: We have made some of you a trial for others.
phrases.explanation: The verse then explains why messengers were made ordinary. Some of you have been made a trial for others, and the commentary presents this as part of the design rather than an accident. A messenger who needs food can be doubted, and that doubt is the test. The worldly difference between prophet and people becomes the very thing that separates those who believe from those who wait for a sign.

phrases.translation: Will you ˹not then˺ be patient?
phrases.explanation: The question that follows names the response being asked for. Will you not then be patient? Patience is asked of the believers, since the trial described is not a punishment but a test they are expected to endure. The verse does not promise that the difficulty will be removed. It asks whether the people being tested will accept the conditions under which the test is run.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is All-Seeing
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with the statement that makes patience reasonable. Your Lord is All-Seeing, and the commentary applies this to the whole situation, the messengers, the mockers, and those who wait for proof. Nothing of what anyone does is unnoticed. The reminder gives the trial a witness and an end, since what is seen will be judged by the One who saw it.

phrases.translation: Those who do not expect to meet Us say,
phrases.explanation: The verse identifies the speakers by what they do not expect. Those who do not expect to meet Us are the ones making the demand that follows, and the commentary explains them as people who neither fear the meeting with Allah nor dread His punishment. The description comes first because it explains the request. People who have no expectation of standing before their Lord can ask for any proof without fearing what it would cost them.

phrases.translation: “If only the angels were sent down to us, or we could see our Lord!”
phrases.explanation: The demand is for a different kind of revelation. If only the angels had been sent down to us, or we could see our Lord, and the commentary explains the request as their wanting angels to confirm that Muhammad spoke the truth, or wanting to see Allah tell them Himself. Either way they ask to be addressed directly rather than through a messenger. The condition they set is one that no prophet was ever given.

phrases.translation: They have certainly been carried away by their arrogance and have entirely exceeded all limits
phrases.explanation: The verse then names the fault behind the demand. They have been carried away by their arrogance and have exceeded all limits, and the commentary explains this as their deeming themselves great and overstepping the bounds of arrogance by the very words they spoke. The request is not humble enquiry but self-importance. What looks like a demand for certainty is diagnosed as a refusal to accept a rank they did not choose.

phrases.translation: ˹But˺ on the Day they will see the angels, there will be no good news for the wicked,
phrases.explanation: The day they asked for arrives with the opposite result. When they see the angels, there is no good news for the wicked, and the commentary explains the good tidings as the news they would have wanted and will not receive. The verse grants their request in form while denying its purpose. Seeing angels was supposed to settle the matter in their favour, and instead it settles it against them.

phrases.translation: who will cry, “Keep away! Away ˹from us˺!”
phrases.explanation: The cry that follows is explained in two ways. The commentary prefers the reading in which the angels say it to the criminals, declaring that good news is forbidden and barred from them. Others take it as the words of the polytheists seeking refuge. The preference is argued from the meaning of the word, since it denotes a prohibition rather than a request for protection. Either way the door to good news is shut.

phrases.translation: Then We will turn to whatever ˹good˺ deeds they did,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes what happens to their deeds. We will turn to whatever good they did, and the commentary explains the phrase as Allah proceeding to the works these criminals performed. The word carries the sense of advancing toward something in order to deal with it. Their record is not ignored but examined, which makes what follows a judgement rather than a dismissal.

phrases.translation: reducing them to scattered dust
phrases.explanation: The deeds are then reduced to scattered dust, and the commentary explains the image as the motes visible in a shaft of sunlight, which the hand cannot grasp and which disappear in the shade. It also explains why this happens, that the works were done for other than Allah. The comparison is exact, since what looked substantial while the light fell on it turns out to be nothing that can be held.

phrases.translation: ˹But˺ on that Day the residents of Paradise will have the best settlement and
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to the other side of the comparison. On that Day the residents of Paradise will have the best settlement, and the commentary explains this as their dwelling in the garden being better than the dwelling of those who boasted of their worldly possessions. The measure is the same as in the earlier verse, where a settlement was named for the people of the fire. The two endings are placed side by side again, and the better one is identified.

phrases.translation: the finest place to rest
phrases.explanation: The resting place is added to the settlement. They will have the finest place to rest, and the commentary takes up the question of whether there is a midday rest in the garden, answering that the phrase refers to the rest at the time when people rest in this world. One report says the people of the garden experience only the span of a single day before they take up their dwellings. The wording keeps the description close to something the hearers knew.

phrases.translation: ˹Watch for˺ the Day the heavens will burst with clouds,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes the sky on that Day. The heavens will burst with clouds, and the commentary notes that reciters differ over whether the verb is read with a doubled letter or a softened one, and accepts both as sound readings with the same meaning. It explains the splitting as the heaven opening through a cloud, described as white. The image is of a sky that can no longer hold what is behind it.

phrases.translation: and the angels will be sent down in successive ranks
phrases.explanation: The angels then descend, and the commentary explains this as a real descent to the earth rather than a metaphor. Their coming in successive ranks answers the demand made earlier in the surah, when the objectors asked for angels to be sent down as proof. The request is granted at the moment when proof is no longer useful. What they wanted as confirmation arrives as the beginning of judgement.

phrases.translation: True authority on that Day will belong ˹only˺ to the Most Compassionate.
phrases.explanation: The verse states who holds authority on that Day. True authority belongs only to the Most Compassionate, and the commentary explains this as sovereignty that no one else shares, since every other kingdom has perished. In this life there were kings, and the verse does not deny it, but on that Day their rule is gone. The title chosen is mercy, which is striking in a passage about judgement.

phrases.translation: And it will be a hard day for the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: The day is then described from the other side. It will be a hard day for the disbelievers, and the commentary explains this as a harsh and severe day for those who disbelieved in Allah. The verse sets the softness of the title against the hardness of the experience. The same day is mercy for some and severity for others, and what separates them is not the day but what they did with the message.

phrases.translation: And ˹beware of˺ the Day the wrongdoer will bite his nails ˹in regret˺
phrases.explanation: The verse shows regret in a physical gesture. The wrongdoer bites his nails on the Day of judgement, and the commentary explains this as remorse and grief over what he neglected of Allah's right and over the ruin of his own soul through disbelief. The image is of a person with nothing left to do with his hands. What he is regretting is not a mistake in reasoning but a life spent following someone who turned him away.

phrases.translation: and say, “Oh! I wish I had followed the Way along with the Messenger
phrases.explanation: Then he speaks the wish that has no use left. Oh, I wish I had followed the Way along with the Messenger, and the commentary explains the Way as the road to deliverance from Allah's punishment. The wish is precise, since it names the alternative he could have taken and did not. It also places the messenger at the centre of his regret, because that was the choice set before him in this life.

phrases.translation: Woe to me!
phrases.explanation: The exclamation is short and raw. Woe to me, he cries, and the word is the cry of someone addressing his own ruin rather than complaining about another. The verse lets him speak in his own voice, which makes the scene personal rather than doctrinal. Everything he had defended in public is being undone in one word spoken too late.

phrases.translation: I wish I had never taken so-and-so as a close friend
phrases.explanation: The regret then attaches to a person. I wish I had never taken so-and-so as a close friend, and the commentary reports that some identified the wrongdoer as Uqba ibn Abi Muayt, who returned to disbelief to please Ubayy ibn Khalaf, while others took the friend to mean Satan. The verse leaves the name general so that every reader can recognise his own companion in it. The choice of a friend is being shown as a decision with consequences beyond this life.

phrases.translation: It was he who truly made me stray from the Reminder after it had reached me.”
phrases.explanation: He explains what the friendship did. It was he who made me stray from the Reminder after it had reached me, and the commentary explains the Reminder as the Qur'an and the straying as being turned away from belief in it after it had come from Allah. The verse puts the responsibility on the one who misled without excusing the one who followed. What makes the case so painful is that the guidance had already arrived.

phrases.translation: And Satan has always betrayed humanity
phrases.explanation: The verse then draws the wider lesson. Satan has always betrayed humanity, and the commentary explains the betrayal as forsaking a person in what befalls him, without saving or delivering him. The word describes abandonment at the moment of need. The friend who promised companionship is exposed as belonging to a pattern of promises that end exactly where help is required.

phrases.translation: The Messenger has cried, “O my Lord!
phrases.explanation: The scene shifts from the wrongdoer to the messenger. The Messenger has cried to his Lord, and the commentary places this cry on the same day, which sets the two voices side by side. One is a lament over a wasted life and the other is a complaint about a people who would not listen. The verse makes the messenger's grief part of the judgement scene rather than a private sorrow.

phrases.translation: My people have indeed received this Quran with neglect.”
phrases.explanation: What he reports is that his people received the Qur'an with neglect, and the commentary records two explanations, that they spoke evil of it and called it sorcery and poetry, and that they abandoned it and refused to listen. The commentary prefers the second, citing the verse in which they told people not to listen to it. The word covers both mockery and indifference, and both are ways of taking a message as though it did not matter.

phrases.translation: Similarly, We made enemies for every prophet from among the wicked,
phrases.explanation: The verse consoles the messenger with a pattern. Enemies were made for every prophet from among the wicked, and the commentary explains this as Allah telling him that what he faced was not unique to him. Prophets before him met the same opposition from the same kind of people. The purpose is patience, and the verse points to those of firm resolve among earlier messengers as the example to follow.

phrases.translation: but sufficient is your Lord as a Guide and Helper
phrases.explanation: The second half supplies what the messenger needs to keep going. Sufficient is your Lord as a Guide and Helper, and the commentary explains the first as Allah guiding him to the truth and the straight path, and the second as His support against his enemies. The two roles answer two different needs, clarity about the way and strength against those who oppose it. The verse also tells him not to let his enemies frighten him.

phrases.translation: The disbelievers say, “If only the Quran had been sent down to him all at once!”
phrases.explanation: The objection concerns the delivery of the book rather than its content. If only the whole Qur'an had been sent down at once, and the commentary explains that they compared it with the Torah, which came down upon Moses in one piece. The demand is for a single dramatic event rather than a drawn-out process. They are asking for revelation on their own terms, in the form that would most impress them.

phrases.translation: ˹We have sent it˺ as such ˹in stages˺ so We may reassure your heart with it.
phrases.explanation: The answer explains the staged sending. It came down in this way to reassure the heart, and the commentary explains this as verse by verse, one after another, strengthening the Prophet as he received it. A book arriving in pieces accompanies a life lived under pressure, whereas a single delivery would have been a spectacle. The form of the revelation is thus matched to the work it had to do.

phrases.translation: And We have revealed it at a deliberate pace
phrases.explanation: The final phrase describes the manner of the sending. It has been revealed at a deliberate pace, and the commentary explains this as teaching it piece by piece until it was known by heart, with deliberation in recitation. Another explanation gives it as exposition and clear explanation. The slowness is not weakness but the condition for being understood and carried, and the verse turns the objection into a description of care.

phrases.translation: Whenever they bring you an argument,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes a continuous exchange. Whenever the objectors bring an argument, an answer comes, and the commentary keeps the two sides facing each other. The word for argument covers objections of every kind, whether about the messenger's humanity or the book's origin. The verse assumes that the objections will keep coming and that each one will meet a response rather than silence.

phrases.translation: We come to you with the right refutation and the best explanation
phrases.explanation: The response is described as the right refutation and the best explanation, and the commentary explains this as an answer that is both correct and clearer than the argument it answers. The two qualities matter, since a reply can be true but badly put. The verse sets the pattern for the whole chapter, which answers one accusation after another. It also tells the Prophet that he does not have to invent the answers.

phrases.translation: Those who will be dragged into Hell on their faces
phrases.explanation: The verse names the destination of those who argued. They will be dragged into Hell on their faces, and the commentary keeps the image as it stands, a posture of utter humiliation rather than of walking. Being pulled face down says that they arrive without dignity and without choice. The people who demanded to see Allah are described as unable even to stand upright.

phrases.translation: will be in the worst place, and are ˹now˺ farthest from the ˹Right˺ Way
phrases.explanation: The verse then sets their position twice over. They are in the worst place and farthest from the right way, and the commentary explains the two descriptions as belonging together, since a bad destination follows from a wrong road. Having spent the passage answering the objections one by one, the verse summarises where the objectors had ended up. The judgement is a statement of fact rather than an insult.

phrases.translation: We certainly gave Moses the Book
phrases.explanation: The verse begins a series of reminders. We certainly gave Moses the Book, and the commentary identifies the Book as the Torah and notes that it was given to him just as the Criterion was given to Muhammad. The comparison is placed at the start of a passage about peoples who rejected their messengers. Mentioning Moses first sets up both the pattern of opposition and the pattern of rescue.

phrases.translation: and appointed his brother Aaron as his helper
phrases.explanation: The verse adds the support given to him. His brother Aaron was appointed as his helper, and the commentary explains the word as a helper and a supporter. The task was not laid on one man alone, which answers the objection raised earlier about a messenger needing human company. What the objectors treated as a defect in the Prophet is shown to have been the pattern with earlier messengers too.

phrases.translation: We had ordered ˹them˺, “Go to the people who would deny Our signs.”
phrases.explanation: The command that follows is quoted. Go to the people who would deny Our signs, and the commentary explains the people as Pharaoh and his court, who rejected the messages and the proofs brought to them. The verse reports the command and the outcome without describing the journey. That compression keeps the focus on the certainty of what happened to those who denied.

phrases.translation: Then We annihilated the deniers entirely
phrases.explanation: The outcome is total. Then We annihilated the deniers entirely, and the commentary notes that something has been left out between the command and the destruction, namely that the two went, were rejected, and were then vindicated. The gap is filled from the context, as is common in the Qur'an's narration. The verse offers the pattern in miniature for the people of Mecca to consider.

phrases.translation: And when the people of Noah rejected the messengers, We drowned them, making them an example to humanity.
phrases.explanation: The next example is the people of Noah. When they rejected the messengers, We drowned them and made them an example to humanity, and the commentary explains the drowning as the flood and the example as a lesson for all people to take heed from. Rejecting one messenger is described as rejecting the messengers, since every messenger brings the same call. The punishment was visible, memorable, and universal in its warning.

phrases.translation: And We have prepared a painful punishment for the wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: The verse then adds what awaits them beyond this life. A painful punishment has been prepared for the wrongdoers, and the commentary explains that this is in addition to the chastisement that already reached them in this world. The drowning was not the end of the matter. The verse separates the visible destruction from the final reckoning, and both are presented as the consequence of the same rejection.

phrases.translation: Also ˹We destroyed˺ ’Ȃd, Thamûd, and the people of the Water-pit,
phrases.explanation: More peoples are named. Ad, Thamud, and the people of the Water-pit are added to the list, and the commentary records the disagreement over who the last of these were, some placing them among Thamud, some in a village of Yamama, and some saying they were a people who buried their prophet in a well. The commentary prefers the view that they lived by a well, since the word denotes anything dug. The name is kept as the Qur'an gives it.

phrases.translation: as well as many peoples in between
phrases.explanation: The verse closes the list with those left unnamed. Many peoples in between were also destroyed, and the commentary explains this as generations between the named ones whose number is known to Allah alone. Naming a few and leaving the rest unnumbered keeps the pattern from becoming a closed list. The point is not the exact count but the repetition of the same end for the same refusal.

phrases.translation: For each We set forth
phrases.explanation: The verse states the method before the destruction. For each We set forth various lessons, and the commentary explains this as laying out the examples, drawing attention to the proofs, and excusing Himself before them by means of admonition. No people was destroyed before the case had been put to them fully. The verse answers any suggestion that the punishment came without warning.

phrases.translation: ˹various˺ lessons, and We ultimately destroyed each
phrases.explanation: The second half states the result. We ultimately destroyed each, and the commentary explains the word as exterminating them root and branch, putting an end to them all. The same care was shown to each and the same end came to each. The verse holds the two truths together, that the warning was complete and that the destruction was complete, so that neither mercy nor justice is left in doubt.

phrases.translation: They have certainly passed by the city ˹of Sodom˺, which had been showered with a dreadful rain ˹of stones˺.
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to a sight the hearers knew. They have certainly passed by the city that was showered with a dreadful rain, and the commentary identifies the city as Sodom, the city of Lot's people, and the rain as the stones rained down on them. Their ruins stood on a travelled road, so the evidence was not remote history but something they saw. The verse asks whether they had not looked at it.

phrases.translation: Have they not seen its ruins? But they do not expect to be resurrected
phrases.explanation: The question is followed by the reason it does no good. Have they not seen its ruins, yet they do not expect to be resurrected, and the commentary explains that they pass the site without drawing the lesson because they deny the raising of the dead. Other verses in this passage treat them as no better than cattle that do not understand. The ruins could warn them only if they believed that a reckoning was coming.

phrases.translation: When they see you ˹O Prophet˺, they only make fun of you,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes how they receive him. When they see you, they only make fun of you, and the commentary explains that the mockery was their habitual response whenever he appeared. The messenger himself becomes the joke rather than the message. This is the form opposition takes when a person has no argument left, and the surah has already shown them failing to produce one.

phrases.translation: ˹saying,˺ “Is this the one that Allah has sent as a messenger
phrases.explanation: The mockery is then quoted. Is this the one Allah has sent as a messenger, they ask, and the commentary adds the sneer that he was sent above all His creatures. The question is not a request for information but a way of belittling him, made sharper by the fact that he was one of their own townsmen. They cannot deny that he claims a mission, so they make the claim ridiculous instead.

phrases.translation: He would have almost tricked us away from our gods, had we not been so devoted to them.”
phrases.explanation: Their own words are turned into a confession. He would have almost tricked us away from our gods, had we not been so devoted to them, and the commentary explains this as their admission that his argument nearly moved them and that only stubbornness held them. They call his case a trick because it almost worked. What they present as loyalty to their gods is described as endurance in a position they cannot defend.

phrases.translation: ˹But˺ soon they will know, when they face the punishment, who is far astray from the ˹Right˺ Way
phrases.explanation: The verse then answers them with a warning. Soon they will know, when they face the punishment, who is far astray from the right way, and the commentary explains that it will become clear to them when they see the punishment whether the one astray was the messenger or themselves. The mockery and the claim of steadfastness are left to be resolved at the moment of seeing. The question they asked in scorn is turned back on them.

phrases.translation: Have you seen ˹O Prophet˺ the one who has taken their own desires as their god?
phrases.explanation: The verse turns from mockery to a deeper diagnosis. Have you seen the one who has taken his own desires as a god, and the commentary explains the background of a man who would worship a stone and exchange it for a prettier one, so that his god was whatever he chose for himself. This is worship without a standard outside the worshipper. The person who laughed at a messenger is shown to be obeying nothing but his own preference.

phrases.translation: Will you then be a keeper over them
phrases.explanation: The verse then asks the Prophet a question about responsibility. Will you be a keeper over them, and the commentary explains the word as guardian of their deeds, asked in a way that shows the impossibility of the task given the depth of their ignorance. He is not told to force them into belief. The verse relieves him of a burden he never carried, since guidance belongs to Allah and not to the warner.

phrases.translation: Or do you think that most of them listen or understand?
phrases.explanation: The verse questions what the hearers are actually doing. Do you think that most of them listen or understand, and the commentary explains that the question concerns whether they attend to the recitation and grasp the proofs set before their eyes. The answer is expected to be no. Hearing and understanding are separated here, because a person may hear words without ever allowing them to reach a conclusion.

phrases.translation: They are only like cattle—no, more than that, they are astray from the ˹Right˺ Way
phrases.explanation: The comparison that follows is severe. They are only like cattle, no, more astray from the right way, and the commentary explains the difference, since cattle find their pasture and obey their owners, while these people do not obey their Lord and do not acknowledge the favours given to them. The image is not of stupidity but of refusal. An animal follows the one who provides for it, and the argument is that they do not.

phrases.translation: Have you not seen how your Lord extends
phrases.explanation: The verse offers a sign in something ordinary. Have you not seen how your Lord extends, and the commentary explains the shade that is extended as the period between the breaking of dawn and the rising of the sun, when light is spread without a defined edge. It is the hour before the day takes shape, and everyone has watched it without thinking to question it. The question is addressed to sight rather than to argument.

phrases.translation: the shade—He could have simply made it ˹remain˺ still if He so willed—then We make the sun its guide
phrases.explanation: The rest of the verse explains what holds the shade in place. He could have made it remain still if He willed, so that it would never recede, and then He made the sun its guide, since the sun shows the shadow for what it is. The commentary notes that a thing is known by its opposite, as sweetness is known through sourness. Without the sun driving the shade away, no one would know it existed. What fades on schedule is a creation under command.

phrases.translation: causing the shade to retreat gradually
phrases.explanation: This short verse finishes the image. The shade is drawn back gradually, and the commentary records two readings of the last word, one taking it as quick and the other as hidden, with the boundary between sun and shade described as fine as a thread. Either way the withdrawal is so smooth that it cannot be caught in the act. The verse leaves the reader with a process too quiet to notice and too steady to be an accident.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who has made the night for you as a cover,
phrases.explanation: The verse names the One behind the sign. He is the One Who has made the night for you as a cover, and the commentary explains the image as a shelter in which creatures take refuge and find rest, compared to clothing that covers a person. The night is not merely an absence of light but something given for a purpose. The same hand that stretched the shade is described as covering and settling those who live under it.

phrases.translation: and ˹made˺ sleep for resting,
phrases.explanation: Sleep is added as a second gift. He made sleep for resting, and the commentary explains this as the means by which bodies revive and limbs are stilled. Sleep is placed in the same sentence as the night that carries it, so that the two are seen as one provision. Something the reader does every day is presented as evidence, not as a routine fact to be passed over.

phrases.translation: and the day for rising
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with the day and its purpose. He made the day for rising, and the commentary explains the word as awakening and coming back to life, noting the same root used for the raising of the dead and the prayer said when rising from sleep. Another explanation gives it as the time when people disperse for their livelihood. Either way the day is not the opposite of the night but its resumption, and the verse closes the cycle of covering, resting, and rising.

phrases.translation: And He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy,
phrases.explanation: The next sign is in the wind. He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy, and the commentary explains them as the winds that fertilise and announce the rain, going ahead of it as good news. Mercy here is something that arrives over land and is watched for. The winds are given no power of their own but are described as sent, and their work is to carry news of what comes behind them.

phrases.translation: and We send down pure rain from the sky
phrases.explanation: The rain is then described. We send down pure rain from the sky, and the commentary explains it as purifying water brought down from the clouds that were raised up by those winds. The two halves of the verse are connected as cause and provision. Water that cleanses is not a small gift in a land where water is scarce, and the verse names it before describing what it does.

phrases.translation: giving life to a lifeless land,
phrases.explanation: The first purpose of the rain is stated. It gives life to a lifeless land, and the commentary explains the land as parched and barren, bringing forth nothing. The word for dead is used of a place that is inactive rather than of a body, and the commentary notes why the wording follows the place and not the thing. The comparison to resurrection is close at hand, since land that produces again looks like something brought back.

phrases.translation: and providing water for countless animals and humans of Our Own creation
phrases.explanation: The second purpose widens the benefit. It provides water for countless animals and humans of Our Own creation, and the commentary explains that the word covers cattle and great numbers of people. The rain is not sent only for the fields but for everything that drinks. The verse moves from the land to the creatures on it, and the phrase of Our own creation keeps the supply a gift rather than a right.

phrases.translation: We certainly disperse it among them so they may be mindful,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes the distribution of that water. We certainly disperse it among them so they may be mindful, and the commentary records reports that no year has more rain than another but that it is divided among lands and creatures. The point is that the rain arrives by measure and moves around. The purpose named is remembrance, since rain that comes and goes should keep the dependant aware of the One who sends it.

phrases.translation: but most people persist in ungratefulness
phrases.explanation: The verse then reports the response. Most people persist in ungratefulness, and the commentary explains this as denying the favours and rejecting the generosity shown to them, with some mention of those who credited the rain to the stars. The verdict is put at the end of a list of provisions. The failure is not a failure to notice the water but a failure to acknowledge where it came from.

phrases.translation: Had We willed,
phrases.explanation: The verse states a possibility left unused. Had We willed, We could have easily sent a warner, and the commentary explains the point as Allah telling the Prophet that warning could have been distributed so that a warner went to every town. The work given to him was therefore heavier than it had to be. The verse makes the burden he carries a matter of choice rather than necessity.

phrases.translation: We could have easily sent a warner to every society
phrases.explanation: The verse names the scope of that burden. A warner to every society would have shared the labour, but he was sent to all of them together, and the commentary explains that the reward for bearing this lies with Allah. The heaviness is not hidden or softened. It is presented as the reason for the encouragement that follows, where he is told not to yield and to strive with the Qur'an itself.

phrases.translation: So do not yield to the disbelievers,
phrases.explanation: The command is direct. So do not yield to the disbelievers, and the commentary explains this as refusing what they called him to, the worship of their gods, and warns of the doubling of punishment if he did. The verse treats the pressure as real and the refusal as a decision to be made rather than a mood to be maintained. It also makes clear that the temptation was not only persecution but compromise.

phrases.translation: but strive diligently against them with this ˹Quran˺
phrases.explanation: The means of resistance is then named. Strive diligently against them with this Quran, and the commentary records that the striving intended is by the Qur'an itself, with a great striving, until they accept what it obliges and are guided by it. The weapon given is the book he is told to deliver, not the sword. The verse sets the whole campaign inside the recitation and its argument, which is why the surah has spent so long answering objections.

phrases.translation: And He is the One Who merges the two bodies of water:
phrases.explanation: The verse names another work of the same hand. He is the One Who merges the two bodies of water, and the commentary explains the root as mixing, since the two seas are brought together and flow into one another. It also notes that the same root gives the word for a meadow where animals of every kind are gathered. The image is of two things meeting at close quarters, not of two things kept far apart.

phrases.translation: one fresh and palatable and the other salty and bitter,
phrases.explanation: The two waters are then described by taste. One is fresh and palatable and the other is salty and bitter, and the commentary explains the sweet water as the rivers and the rain, and the bitter as the seas. It also explains the purpose, that people could drink from the sweet while living beside the salt. The distinction is one every traveller knows, and the verse treats the difference as a deliberate arrangement.

phrases.translation: placing between them a barrier they cannot cross
phrases.explanation: The last phrase states the restraint. Between them a barrier is placed that they cannot cross, and the commentary explains this as a partition preventing each from corrupting the other, with the salt forbidden to spoil the sweet. Reports are quoted describing a divider no eye can see, with the two meeting and not mixing. The verse names the limit as a decree, not as an accident of geography.

phrases.translation: And He is the One Who creates human beings from a ˹humble˺ liquid,
phrases.explanation: The verse moves from water to the one made from it. He creates human beings from a humble liquid, and the commentary explains the drop from which a person is formed. From that small beginning a whole web of relations is produced, which the rest of the verse sets out. The pairing of a humble origin with an extensive result is the argument of the passage, since the One who begins a life can also raise it again.

phrases.translation: then establishes for them bonds of kinship and marriage.
phrases.explanation: The verse then names what is established from that beginning. Bonds of kinship and marriage are set up for them, and the commentary distinguishes the two, counting the categories of blood relation and those created by marriage. These ties are the fabric of a society, and the verse presents them as given rather than invented. Something so ordinary as family is placed among the signs of the Creator's power.

phrases.translation: For your Lord is Most Capable
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with the ground of it all. Your Lord is Most Capable, and the commentary explains this as the power to create what He wishes and to guide whom He intends. The word answers any doubt about the raising of the dead, since the One who made a person from a drop and built a family around him is not limited by the first beginning. The verse ends as the previous one did, on capability.

phrases.translation: Yet they worship besides Allah what can neither benefit nor harm them.
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to the contradiction. They worship beside Allah what can neither benefit nor harm them, and the commentary explains that these gods give nothing when served and take nothing when neglected. The list of provisions just recited makes the charge sharper, since everything they have came from the One they ignore. The accusation is not that their gods are weak but that they are nothing.

phrases.translation: And the disbeliever always collaborates against their Lord
phrases.explanation: The verse then names the company the disbeliever keeps. He always collaborates against his Lord, and the commentary explains this as helping Satan in disobedience, with reports naming Abu Jahl as an example. It records another view, that the word means the disbeliever is of little account with his Lord, and rejects it in favour of the first. Either way the verse ends the passage by showing whose side the ingratitude serves.

phrases.translation: And We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a deliverer
phrases.explanation: The verse states the limit of the messenger's task. We have sent you only as a deliverer, and the commentary explains that the good news is the reward promised to whoever believes in him and acts on what he brought. The word only narrows the mission against every expectation that a messenger would bring power or wealth. He is a bearer of a report, and the report is what people will be judged by.

phrases.translation: of good news and a warner
phrases.explanation: The second role is added to the first. He is a warner, and the commentary explains the warning as directed to whoever denies him and refuses what he brought. Good news and warning are one message seen from two sides, since the same announcement is comfort to one hearer and threat to another. The verse keeps both, which is why the Prophet cannot be reduced to either a comforter or an accuser.

phrases.translation: Say, “I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺,
phrases.explanation: The messenger is told to state his position openly. Say, I do not ask you for any reward for this message, and the commentary explains that he was answering the suspicion that he wanted their wealth and would not be followed unless he dropped the demand for it. The verse clears the messenger of a motive that would have made his call look like a transaction. What he brings costs him something and gains him nothing from them.

phrases.translation: but whoever wishes, let them pursue the Way to their Lord.”
phrases.explanation: The verse then leaves the choice with the hearer. Whoever wishes, let them pursue the Way to their Lord, and the commentary explains the way as a path taken toward Him through spending wealth and doing good, including giving alms and supporting the struggle. No one is paid to accept and no one is compelled. The invitation is open, and the cost of taking it falls on the person who chooses to walk.

phrases.translation: Put your trust in the Ever-Living, Who never dies,
phrases.explanation: The command is to rely on the One who cannot be lost. Put your trust in the Ever-Living, Who never dies, and the commentary explains this as committing the matter to Him, submitting to Him, and bearing patiently what comes. Every other support eventually fails, which is precisely the point of the description. The verse gives the Prophet a foundation that does not depend on the response of his people.

phrases.translation: and glorify His praises.
phrases.explanation: Praise is joined to trust. Glorify His praises, and the commentary explains this as worshipping Him in thanks for the favours given. Trust without worship would be a bare resignation, and praise without trust would be words only. The two are placed together because the One relied upon is also the One who is thanked for everything already received.

phrases.translation: Sufficient is He as All-Aware of the sins of His servants
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with what is sufficient. Sufficient is He as All-Aware of the sins of His servants, and the commentary explains that nothing of their deeds is hidden from Him, that He counts them all and will repay them on the Day of Resurrection. The messenger who is mocked can leave the account with the One who knows. No wrong done to him or to the message goes unseen, and the passage rests there.

phrases.translation: ˹He is˺ the One Who created the heavens and the earth and everything in between in six Days,
phrases.explanation: The verse repeats the command to trust by naming the One trusted. He is the One Who created the heavens and the earth and everything in between in six Days, and the commentary notes the wording of between them in the dual though the heavens are plural, since what is meant is the two kinds. The creator of everything is a safe repository for any matter. The measure of six days is given without discussion of what a day was then.

phrases.translation: then established Himself on the Throne.
phrases.explanation: The verse then states the establishment on the Throne, and the commentary explains it as rising over the Throne and being exalted above it, adding that it took place on the day after the completion of creation. The point is stated without elaboration, and the commentary leaves it there. What matters for the passage is that the One who is asked to be trusted is described as the ruler of all that was made.

phrases.translation: ˹He is˺ the Most Compassionate! Ask ˹none other than˺ the All-Knowledgeable about Himself
phrases.explanation: The verse then names Him and gives a command. He is the Most Compassionate, so ask the All-Knowledgeable about Himself, and the commentary explains the instruction as telling the Prophet to ask the One who is fully informed about His creation, since nothing He made is hidden from Him. Another report takes it as a reassurance that whatever Allah informs him of is true. The title Compassionate comes just before the charge to ask about Him.

phrases.translation: When it is said to them, “Prostrate to the Most Compassionate,”
phrases.explanation: The verse reports a specific refusal. When it is said to them, prostrate to the Most Compassionate, and the commentary explains that they were being called to direct worship to Allah alone, away from the gods and idols they served. The command uses the very name they would not accept. The scene takes the argument of the surah from debate about the messenger to the question of who is being worshipped.

phrases.translation: they ask ˹in disgust˺, “What is ‘the Most Compassionate’? Will we prostrate to whatever you order us to?”
phrases.explanation: Their answer is quoted with its contempt. What is the Most Compassionate, they ask, and will we prostrate to whatever you order us to, and the commentary notes that reciters differ over whether the final pronoun is addressed to the Prophet or refers to the Compassionate, and accepts both readings. It also records that a rival in Yamama was called by the same title. Either way the question is a refusal dressed as a request for information.

phrases.translation: And it only drives them farther away
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with the effect of the exchange. It only drives them farther away, and the commentary explains that the call to prostration increased their aversion and made them flee from sincere worship. The reminder does not soften them but hardens them. The verse states this plainly, and it prepares the contrast that comes later in the surah, where the true servants of the Compassionate are described.

phrases.translation: Blessed is the One Who has placed constellations in the sky, as well as a ˹radiant˺ lamp
phrases.explanation: The verse returns to the sky. Blessed is the One Who has placed constellations in the sky, and the commentary records two views, one taking them as palaces in the heaven where watchers reside and the other as great stars, and prefers the first since that is the usage of the language. A lamp is then named, explained as the sun, with reciters differing over whether the word is singular or plural. Blessing belongs to the One who arranged it all.

phrases.translation: and a luminous moon
phrases.explanation: The verse finishes with the moon. A luminous moon is added to the sun, and the commentary explains the word as one that gives light. The pairing of a lamp and a moon keeps the two sources distinct rather than merging them. After the objection about the Compassionate, the verses point again to the order of the sky, which the objectors saw every night and could not claim to have made.

phrases.translation: And He is the One Who causes the day and the night to alternate,
phrases.explanation: The verse names another arrangement. He is the One Who causes the day and the night to alternate, and the commentary records three explanations of the word, that each replaces the other so missed worship can be made up, that each is the opposite of the other in colour, and that each follows the other as it departs. The last is the plain sense and the most useful. What is described is a rhythm rather than a static pair.

phrases.translation: ˹as a sign˺ for whoever desires to be mindful
phrases.explanation: The purpose of the alternation is then given. It is a sign for whoever desires to be mindful, and the commentary explains the sign as a proof for whoever wants to remember the matter of Allah and return to the truth. The benefit is not automatic. The turning of day into night is offered to everyone, and only the person who wants to notice takes anything from it.

phrases.translation: or to be grateful
phrases.explanation: The second kind of person is added. Whoever desires to be grateful, and the commentary explains this as acknowledging the favour of Allah in the changing course of night and day. Remembrance and gratitude are the two responses the sign can produce, one about who God is and the other about what He has given. The verse ends by naming both, which leaves the reader with the question of which one he is.

phrases.translation: The ˹true˺ servants of the Most Compassionate are those who walk on the earth humbly,
phrases.explanation: The verse begins a long portrait of a different kind of person. The true servants of the Most Compassionate are those who walk on the earth humbly, and the commentary explains this as walking with gentleness, tranquillity, and dignity, without haughtiness or corruption. It also records views that the humility is obedience and that it is the refusal to harm anyone. The ones who refused to bow are now contrasted with those whose whole bearing is lowly.

phrases.translation: and when the foolish address them ˹improperly˺, they only respond with peace
phrases.explanation: The verse adds how they answer abuse. When the foolish address them improperly, they only respond with peace, and the commentary explains this as answering offensive words with a fitting reply and a righteous answer, without rage. The word for foolish means those ignorant of Allah rather than those lacking intelligence. The portrait is of people whose calm is not weakness but a discipline, and the surah continues describing them in the verses that follow.

phrases.translation: ˹They are˺ those who spend ˹a good portion of˺ the night,
phrases.explanation: The description of the servants continues with how they use the night. They spend a good portion of it in worship, and the commentary explains the spending as time given over to prayer rather than wealth. The night is the part of life easiest to keep for oneself, which is why it is named first. What was earlier described as a covering and a rest is here turned into an opportunity to stand before the One who made it.

phrases.translation: prostrating themselves and standing before their Lord
phrases.explanation: The two postures are then named. They prostrate themselves and stand before their Lord, and the commentary explains these as the two positions of the prayer, with the plural forms noting those who do each. Prostration and standing cover the whole movement of the ritual, from the lowest posture to the upright one. The phrase before their Lord places the whole act in His presence rather than in public view.

phrases.translation: ˹They are˺ those who pray, “Our Lord! Keep the punishment of Hell away from us,
phrases.explanation: Their night prayer has a subject. They ask their Lord to turn the punishment of Hell away from them, and the commentary explains the request as a plea made out of fear and dread of Him. The prayer is not only praise but a request for safety, which keeps the servant aware of what he deserves. The words are quoted as part of their description, so the fear is being presented as one of their qualities.

phrases.translation: for its punishment is indeed unrelenting
phrases.explanation: The reason for the plea is then given. Its punishment is indeed unrelenting, and the commentary explains the word as a calamity that clings to whoever bears it and never leaves, like a debt that cannot be repaid. It also records the comparison of the people of Hell as debtors who can never discharge what they owe. The verse makes the fear reasonable, since the danger described has no end.

phrases.translation: It is certainly an evil place to settle and reside.”
phrases.explanation: This short verse completes the prayer. It is certainly an evil place to settle and reside, and the commentary explains both words as dwelling and staying, so that the badness is not only of arrival but of permanence. The servants of the Compassionate ask to be kept from a home rather than from an event. The prayer ends where the description of the fire ends elsewhere in the surah, with a place that no one would choose to remain in.

phrases.translation: ˹They are˺ those who spend neither wastefully nor stingily,
phrases.explanation: The verse names another mark of these servants. When they spend they are neither wasteful nor stingy, and the commentary records two readings of the standard, one taking waste as any spending in disobedience to Allah however small, and the other taking it as exceeding what is needed. It also notes that withholding what is due is the opposite fault. The verse treats money as a test with two ways to fail and only one way to pass.

phrases.translation: but moderately in between
