phrases.explanation: The middle course is then named. They spend moderately in between, and the commentary records sayings that describe the mean, such as a shelter that keeps off sun and rain, food that stills hunger without reaching fullness, and clothing that covers and warms. It also reports the view that the good lies between two evils. The measure is need and obedience rather than a fixed sum, and the verse leaves neither extravagance nor miserliness room to hide.

phrases.translation: ˹They are˺ those who do not invoke any other god besides Allah,
phrases.explanation: The next description is about worship. They do not invoke any other god besides Allah, and the commentary explains that they purify worship for Him alone and devote obedience to Him. The contrast is with the polytheists whose practices the surah has been answering since its opening verses. The first mark of the servants is therefore the one thing their opponents refused, that no partner shares His worship.

phrases.translation: nor take a ˹human˺ life—made sacred by Allah—except with ˹legal˺ right,
phrases.explanation: Life is then protected. They do not take a life made sacred by Allah except with legal right, and the commentary names the cases in which taking life is permitted, such as disbelief after Islam, adultery after marriage, or the taking of a life that is then punished by death. The sanctity of life is stated first and the exception second. The verse treats the exception as narrow and defined rather than open to private judgement.

phrases.translation: nor commit fornication. And whoever does ˹any of˺ this will face the penalty
phrases.explanation: Fornication is named next, and then the general rule. Nor commit fornication, and whoever does any of this will face the penalty, and the commentary explains the penalty as a chastisement and an exemplary punishment from Allah. It also records that the verse was sent down concerning people who had committed such sins before Islam and feared they could not be forgiven. The verse states the consequence and, in what follows, opens the door of repentance.

phrases.translation: Their punishment will be multiplied on the Day of Judgment,
phrases.explanation: The verse spells out that penalty. Their punishment will be multiplied on the Day of Judgment, and the commentary notes that reciters differ over the reading of the two verbs, most making them follow the earlier word while one reads them as beginning a new sentence. It also explains why the connected reading is preferred. The punishment is not a single payment but something increased, which matches the seriousness of the sins named.

phrases.translation: and they will remain in it forever, in disgrace
phrases.explanation: The verse adds duration and shame. They will remain in it forever, in disgrace, and the commentary explains this as abiding without end in humiliation. The two halves of the sentence answer two different fears, one about how long the punishment lasts and the other about how it will feel. Having stated the worst, the passage prepares the exception that follows for those who turn back.

phrases.translation: As for those who repent, believe, and do good deeds,
phrases.explanation: The verse opens the door that the previous warning seemed to shut. As for those who repent, believe, and do good deeds, and the commentary explains repentance as returning from those sins to obedience, belief as affirming what the Prophet brought, and good deeds as acting on the commands and avoiding the prohibitions. Three things are named because a change of direction needs all three. The exception answers the fear of those who thought their past had closed the matter.

phrases.translation: they are the ones whose evil deeds Allah will change into good deeds.
phrases.explanation: The promise is then made specific. They are the ones whose evil deeds Allah will change into good deeds, and the commentary records one view that the change happens in this life, with shirk exchanged for faith and fornication for chastity, and another that evil deeds are replaced with good ones on the Day of Resurrection. It prefers the first, since a past act cannot become its opposite in itself. The verse describes a transformation of the person rather than a rewriting of history.

phrases.translation: For Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with the two names that make the promise possible. Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, and the commentary explains this as forgiveness for whoever repents and mercy that withholds punishment after the return. Forgiveness covers what is past and mercy covers what is to come. The same surah that described a doubled and endless punishment now names a mercy that can replace a whole record.

phrases.translation: And whoever repents and does good
phrases.explanation: The verse restates the condition plainly. Whoever repents and does good, and the commentary explains the two halves as turning from shirk to belief in Allah and His messenger, and acting on what He commands in obedience. Repentance is not treated as a feeling or a statement but as a change that shows in conduct. The verse repeats the terms of the exception so that no one supposes a mere regret is enough.

phrases.translation: has truly turned to Allah properly
phrases.explanation: The result is then named. Such a person has truly turned to Allah properly, and the commentary explains that the promise given to those who repented earlier applies to him as well, that his evil deeds in shirk are exchanged for good deeds in Islam. The word used for turning is the same root as the word for repentance. The verse closes by describing the return itself as the achievement, not only the reward that follows it.

phrases.translation: ˹They are˺ those who do not bear false witness,
phrases.explanation: The description turns to speech and company. They do not bear false witness, and the commentary explains the word for falsehood broadly, as shirk, as lies, and as song, and argues that all of these share the quality of making something appear other than it is. The servants are described by what they refuse to attend rather than only by what they do. Their honesty is shown in the testimony they will not give.

phrases.translation: and when they come across falsehood, they pass ˹it˺ by with dignity
phrases.explanation: The verse then describes how they pass by what is vain. When they come across falsehood, they pass it by with dignity, and the commentary records explanations of vain talk as the hurtful words of the polytheists, as indecent speech, and as any act of disobedience, with the dignified passing as turning away and overlooking it. They neither join in nor preach at every occasion. The verse presents restraint as a form of honour rather than of weakness.

phrases.translation: ˹They are˺ those who, when reminded of the revelation of their Lord,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes their response to reminders. When they are reminded of the revelation of their Lord, they do not turn away, and the commentary explains that they are not like the deaf who do not hear or the blind who do not see, but rather hearts that understand and minds that grasp. The contrast is with people who were present when the verses were recited and remained untouched. Hearing is measured here by what it produces.

phrases.translation: do not turn a blind eye or a deaf ear to it
phrases.explanation: The verse states the same thing a second way, in the image of falling. They do not fall down upon it deaf and blind, and the commentary explains the idiom as meaning that they do not remain in that condition, since the Arabs say a man sat or stood doing something to mean that he continued in it. The reminder does not flatten them into indifference. The verse answers the objection that such language belongs only to unbelievers who reject what they hear.

phrases.translation: ˹They are˺ those who pray, “Our Lord! Bless us with ˹pious˺ spouses and offspring
phrases.explanation: The verse gives their prayer about the people closest to them. Our Lord, bless us with pious spouses and offspring, and the commentary explains the request as asking to be shown that those nearest to them obey Allah, since a believer whose family is upright finds his eye comforted. The prayer is not for wealth or health but for the faith of those he lives with. It is a request about what he will see in his own house.

phrases.translation: who will be the joy of our hearts,
phrases.explanation: The joy of the heart is then named. They ask for offspring who will be the joy of our hearts, and the commentary records a report that this refers to this world rather than the next, and another describing a believer who sees his wife and child obeying Allah. It also records the grief of a man whose son or brother remained a disbeliever. The comfort asked for is not affection but shared obedience.

phrases.translation: and make us models for the righteous.”
phrases.explanation: The prayer ends with a request about others. Make us models for the righteous, and the commentary records two views, that they asked to become leaders whom later generations follow, or that they asked to be an example for the God-fearing. It prefers the first since they asked to lead rather than to be led. The verse closes the portrait with a person who wants his own household and then others to be guided through him.

phrases.translation: It is they who will be rewarded with ˹elevated˺ mansions ˹in Paradise˺ for their perseverance,
phrases.explanation: The verse names what all these qualities earn. It is they who will be rewarded with elevated mansions in Paradise, and the commentary explains the word as an exalted dwelling among the dwellings of Paradise, given for the deeds described. The reward is a home rather than a payment, which fits a passage that has been about households and the people in them. Those who made their houses places of prayer are given houses in return.

phrases.translation: and will be received with salutations and ˹greetings of˺ peace
phrases.explanation: The verse then adds the welcome. They will be received with salutations and greetings of peace, and the commentary notes that reciters differ over the reading of the verb, some taking it as the angels greeting them and others as their meeting that greeting, and accepts both as sound. The peace named here answers the abuse the servants ignored on earth. Those who answered insult with a word of peace are themselves greeted with peace.

phrases.translation: staying there forever.
phrases.explanation: The verse states the duration first. They will stay there forever, and the commentary explains this as remaining eternally without end. The permanence is placed before the description of the place, as though to settle the question of whether such a reward could be lost. Everything the surah has said about the fire's endlessness for the wrongdoers is now matched by an endlessness for the servants, and the second is the one to be sought.

phrases.translation: What an excellent place to settle and reside
phrases.explanation: The verse then praises the place itself. What an excellent place to settle and reside, and the commentary explains both words as dwelling and abiding, the same pair used earlier of the fire when it was called an evil place to settle and reside. The two verses use identical language for opposite homes, so that the contrast is exact. The praise is the last word of the portrait, and it leaves the reader with a considered choice between the two.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “You ˹all˺ would not ˹even˺ matter to my Lord were it not for your faith ˹in Him˺.
phrases.explanation: The surah ends with a command to speak. Say, you would not even matter to my Lord were it not for your faith in Him, and the commentary explains the phrase as a question about what account He would take of them. It also records a reading that takes the word as your supplication, meaning the worship and obedience offered to Him. Faith and calling on Him belong together. A person has weight before Allah for his response to the message.

phrases.translation: But now you ˹disbelievers˺ have denied ˹the truth˺, so the torment is bound to come.”
phrases.explanation: The last words state what remains for those who refuse. But now you have denied the truth, so the torment is bound to come, and the commentary explains the final word as a punishment that clings and does not let go, naming the defeat at Badr as its fulfilment and recording other views. The denial is the reason given and the consequence is certain. The chapter ends with a warning still addressed to those listening.
